2.text: In Koryak, keˊlet of all kinds are called kaˊla, kaˊḷa, kaˊḷak, kaˊmak, also ñiˊnvit, ñênvêˊ-

3.text: tɪčñɪn. The word kaˊmak is used also in Chukchee for the “spirit of disease,” and in the Russo-

4.text: Chukchee jargon for “death” or “dying.” With the Yukaghir, as noted before, a being similar to

5.text: the second class of keˊlet is called a “legendary old man.”¹

6.text: The Asiatic Eskimo call the keˊlᴇ toṛnɪṛak (pl. toṛnɪṛat), which is apparently derived from the

7.text: same root as toṛnak of the American Eskimo. The second class of keˊlet are called by the Asiatic

8.text: Eskimo miraˊxpak, evidently an augmentative. The miraˊxpahit live somewhere on the seashore,

9.text: although it is hard to find their places of habitation. Their footprints, however, are often visible

10.text: on the snow, and are enormously large; but the miraˊxpahit step no farther than an ordinary man.

11.text: The name reˊkkeñ is borrowed by the Eskimo from the Chukchee, and becomes raˊkka in

12.text: the second form of the stem.² With proper phonetical change, vaˊɪrg̣ɪn of the Chukchee becomes

13.text: vahɪˊyñɪn in the northwestern dialect of the Koryak. In Eskimo it is called kɪyaˊṛnaṛak, signifying

14.text: also “being,” and derived from the verb kɪyaṛ-na-kuˊña (“I exist”, “I am”). Tñaˊɪrg̣ɪn (“Morning-

15.text: Dawn”) of the Chukchee becomes Tñahɪˊtñɪn in Koryak. Pičvuˊčin is known to the Koryak under

16.text: the same name, and to the Kamchadal under the name of Pilaˊxčuč. Steller and Krasheninnikoff
